entries.test: Public scientific research available by publication showing whether LLMs had contributed any explanatory insight into why the world or human mind works as it does.
entries.note: The categorical 'anything whatsoever' makes documented explanatory contributions relevant counterexamples.

entries.test: Public comparative studies of contemporary LLM representations and generalization could establish how frequently correct outputs use abstractions shared with humans or symbolic systems on equivalent tasks.
entries.note: Internal computational representations are empirically investigable; 'rarely if ever' asserts frequency rather than uncertainty.

entries.test: Public evaluations across diverse tasks comparing contemporary LLM performance on similar examples and distribution shifts would show whether generalization is broadly fragile and readily broken.
entries.note: 'Can be easily broken' describes an asserted vulnerability, not a probabilistic prediction.

entries.test: The original prompt and response, together with controlled behavioral and mechanistic studies of the relevant model, could establish the counting-and-sorting errors and whether similarity reliance rather than induced abstractions caused them.
entries.note: The example itself is absent from the supplied text. An incorrect answer alone would not establish the proposed cause.

entries.test: The original counting-and-sorting prompt and response would show whether the request had clear, coherent requirements and whether ChatGPT fulfilled them.
entries.note: The surrounding passage supplies a concrete task against which to assess 'up to the job.'

entries.test: The counting-and-sorting exchange and public evaluations of contemporary ChatGPT on related reasoning tasks would show whether it could reliably perform the work discussed.
